items.stem: A one-day 99% Value at Risk of 1 million means:

options.text: On about 1 day in 100, the loss is expected to exceed 1 million
options.rationale: Correct: VaR is a threshold exceeded with the stated small probability.

options.text: The maximum possible loss is exactly 1 million
options.rationale: VaR is not a maximum; losses can exceed it.

options.text: The portfolio will lose 1 million every day
options.rationale: VaR is not a daily certain loss.

options.text: There is zero chance of losing more than 1 million
options.rationale: Losses beyond VaR can and do occur.

items.explanation: Correct: VaR is a threshold exceeded with the stated small probability.

items.stem: Which two are limitations of assuming returns are normally distributed? (Select TWO)

options.text: Real returns show fatter tails (more extreme events) than the normal
options.rationale: Correct: markets exhibit fat tails the normal understates.

options.text: It can understate the probability of large crashes
options.rationale: Correct: the normal underestimates extreme losses.
It does the opposite, understating crashes.

items.stem: The no-arbitrage principle in pricing states that:

options.text: Two assets with identical cash flows should have the same price
options.rationale: Correct: otherwise a riskless profit would be possible.

options.text: Everyone can always earn a guaranteed risk-free profit
options.rationale: No-arbitrage implies such free profits are competed away.
Prices change; no-arbitrage is about consistency, not stasis.
Risk is central to valuation; this is unrelated.
